questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an awareness programme actually changes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an awareness programme can actually change
questions.stem: A ticket asks why phishing click rates barely moved three months after the awareness rollout. Which effect is the programme actually able to produce?

options.text: It stops deceptive messages reaching staff mailboxes by blocking the sending infrastructure.
options.misconception: believes awareness programmes filter inbound phishing mail

options.text: It changes daily habits: staff pause on an urgent request and report it instead of clicking through.
It proves each employee passed a knowledge test, which then justifies closing the ticket.
options.misconception: treats a training pass rate as proof of behaviour change

options.text: It guarantees no credentials will ever be typed on a lookalike domain.
options.misconception: assumes awareness can make phishing attempts impossible

questions.explanation: Awareness changes routines, not the mail path: staff pause before clicking and report afterwards. A flat click rate may reflect harder test messages rather than unchanged staff.
questions.hint: Consider routines and reporting, not mail filtering.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The figure a simulation programme reports that misleads
questions.learningObjective: Read a simulation rate and state what it actually measures
questions.stem: A colleague quotes a simulation where 1,000 messages were sent, 80 were clicked and 60 were reported. What does the quoted figure of 8% actually represent?

options.text: The percentage of staff who would have been compromised, since clicking implies credential theft.
options.misconception: assumes a click always means credentials were captured

options.text: The click-through rate over messages sent, which excludes staff who reported without clicking.
The proportion of messages reported out of the eighty that were clicked.
options.misconception: computes a report rate but labels it as a click rate

options.text: The share of staff who behaved correctly, calculated as reports divided by sends.
options.misconception: treats the report count over sends as a full behaviour score

questions.explanation: 8% is 80 clicks over 1,000 sent, so it describes interaction with the lure rather than data loss or good behaviour. The 60 reports are a separate count and need their own rate beside the click rate.
questions.hint: Divide clicks by sent, then read what it excludes.

questions.topic: A policy exception without an expiry
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an exception needs a review date
questions.stem: One ticket asks the security lead to approve an exception for the payments team. Write the justification you would put in front of the review board.

answer.exemplar: The exception is justified only if it names the compensating control, the exact scope it covers, a review date within a fixed period, and the named owner who can withdraw it, with the risk accepted in writing by the business rather than assumed by default.

questions.explanation: A board can only judge an exception if it knows the scope, the compensating control and the date it ends. An open-ended grant transfers risk silently.
questions.hint: Name the scope, the control and the end date.

questions.stem: A forwarded message raises a question about the remediation schedule. What is the main effect of moving every due date at once?

options.text: It frees engineering capacity because teams no longer switch context between tickets.
options.misconception: believes delay improves focus by batching similar work

options.text: It reduces audit exposure because no ticket is now overdue.
options.misconception: assumes moving dates stops tickets counting as overdue

options.text: It removes the cost of missing a date, so the dates stop driving behaviour.
It lets the programme report a higher completion rate at the quarter boundary.
options.misconception: thinks deadlines affect reporting volume, not behaviour

questions.explanation: A date only disciplines work while missing it carries a cost; when all dates move together, teams learn the date is advisory. Reports may look tidier while the backlog stays exactly the same.
questions.hint: Ask what the deadline is for, not what it looks like.

questions.stem: Two questions decide where a finding lands in the remediation schedule. Choose the pair, then the consequence of using it.

options.text: The language of the advisory and the vendor name; anything else is noise for a small team.
options.misconception: believes vendor wording determines remediation order

options.text: The date the ticket was raised and the engineer's estimate; age always equals urgency.
options.misconception: treats ticket age as a substitute for severity

options.text: The number of tickets in the queue and the seniority of the requester; both drive priority.
options.misconception: assumes queue length and status decide priority

options.text: The technical severity and the business exposure; the pair sets the clock for remediation.

questions.explanation: The schedule ranks on two axes: how serious the weakness is and how much business depends on it, and that pairing sets the patch window. Queue length and requester seniority say nothing about risk.
questions.hint: Risk, not requester status, sets the clock.

questions.topic: The exposure a patch window leaves open
questions.learningObjective: State what remains exploitable during a patch window
questions.stem: A reviewer asks what remains true while a critical flaw sits inside its patch window on an internet-facing host. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Only the confidentiality of data is at risk until the host is rebooted.
options.misconception: narrows the exposure to data theft and ignores admin rights

options.text: Nothing, because the control that detects exploitation opens a compensating gap.
options.misconception: assumes detection closes the exposure it was meant to find

options.text: The flaw stays exploitable until the patch is applied and verified in production.
Risk is fully transferred to the vendor who published the advisory.
options.misconception: believes publishing an advisory transfers risk to its author

questions.explanation: Scheduling shortens the window but does not close the hole, so the flaw stays reachable until the patch is deployed and verified. Detection does not fix anything.
questions.hint: A window limits duration, not exploitability.

questions.stem: The inventory report lists 1,200 assets from January and 1,350 in today's export, after 100 retirements were confirmed. By how much has the inventory grown?

options.text: It grew by 350 assets, treating every new line as a net addition.
options.misconception: adds gross additions without subtracting retirements

options.text: It grew by 150 assets, counting only the additions against the earlier figure.
options.misconception: ignores removals when computing the net change

options.text: It shrank by 100 assets once the confirmed retirements are removed.
options.misconception: treats confirmed retirements as a loss against the count

options.text: It grew by 250 assets, because 150 were added after the 100 retirements.

questions.explanation: Net change is 1,350 minus 1,200, which is 150; adding back the 100 confirmed retirements shows 250 were added in the period. Growth only means something once removals are separated from additions.
questions.hint: Separate additions from removals before comparing.

options.misconception: confuses a missing justification with a missing review date

options.misconception: believes named user details matter more than the expiry date

options.misconception: counts only the service with a public deadline

options.misconception: assumes scanner findings are less reliable than manual ones

options.text: The rating should weigh the gateway's dependents, not the flaw's label alone.

options.text: Applying a real consequence to missed dates and using that consequence once.
Freezing every date for one quarter and reporting the overdue count as it stands.
options.misconception: believes a freeze alone restores urgency

options.misconception: shrinks scope instead of restoring accountability

options.text: Moving only the oldest tickets rather than shifting the whole list.
options.misconception: repeats the pattern of selective extension

questions.explanation: The team has learned dates move, so a freeze without consequence changes nothing. What rebuilds the expectation is a consequence that actually lands once, and selective moves repeat the old pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the residual risk during a patch window
questions.stem: A written description is requested for the risk remaining during a 21-day patch window on critical internet-facing systems. Write the description you would submit.

answer.exemplar: For the window itself the exploitable code is still live, so exposure scales with external reachability, the number of exposed instances and whether compensating controls such as segmentation or a web filter block the path; the honest answer states that residual risk persists until the patch is verified in production, not merely scheduled.

questions.explanation: A window bounds how long the flaw is open, so the description must name reachability, instance count and controls. Scheduling the fix is not removing the risk.
